Doing a direct join to a one-to-many child will multiply city_base rows and thus duplicate any measures derived from city_base. | When composing with other dimension views/tables at the same grain (one-row-per-city), join on city_name. When composing with higher-grain (more granular) tables, either aggregate the granular table to city_name first or perform EXISTS/IN-style filters to avoid row multiplication. | If city_name in other tables can be NULL or have a different normalization, ensure you reconcile/normalize keys (e.g., trim/case) before joining to avoid accidental row mismatches or unintended many-to-one joins.

views.name: cities_by_state_cohort
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.city_name AS city_name,
  city.state_name AS state_name,
  city.population AS population
FROM city

params.description: Provides one row per city with its state and population, allowing queries about city populations and city/state membership.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve population and state for a specific city or list of cities. | Rank or filter cities by population (within the whole dataset or after composing with other views). | Compose into higher-level aggregations (e.g., total population by state) by aggregating the population column. | Join to dimension tables keyed by city_name or state_name when you need attributes without duplicating population measures (see composition guidance).
params.output_schema: city_name: name of the city; derived directly from base column city.city_name. | state_name: name of the state the city belongs to; derived directly from base column city.state_name. | population: numeric population value for the city; derived directly from base column city.population.
params.metric: population = city.population  -- base (atomic) measure at the grain of city (one value per city_name).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a state-level dimension/view (e.g., a view keyed by state_name that has one row per state) on state_name — safe because this view is one-row-per-city and the state-level view is one-row-per-state, so joining will not duplicate the city-level population measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a city-level dimension/view keyed by city_name (one-row-per-city) on city_name — safe because both sides are one-row-per-city and population remains one value per resulting row. | do NOT join to a one-to-many fact table or detail table keyed to city_name (for example a transactions or events table with multiple rows per city) without first aggregating that table to the city level (e.g., SUM(...) GROUP BY city_name). Joining this view directly to a one-to-many table would multiply city rows and thereby duplicate the population measure. | when composing higher-level aggregates (e.g., total population by state), compute SUM(population) GROUP BY state_name on this view rather than relying on joins that would expand rows; this preserves correct totals because population is stored at the city grain. | if you need ratios or rates that combine city.population with counts from another table that is one-to-many to city, first aggregate the other table to city (or to the target grain) so joins remain cardinality-safe.

views.name: state_city_population_agg
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.state_name AS state_name,
  MAX(c.population) AS max_city_population
FROM state s
LEFT JOIN cities_by_state_cohort c
  ON s.state_name = c.state_name
GROUP BY s.state_name

params.description: Per-state maximum city population: for each state_name, the largest population value among cities in that state.
params.when_to_use: Report the largest city population per state (e.g., "what is the max city population in each state?") | Rank or filter states by their largest city (e.g., top N states by max city population) | Compose into higher-level aggregations where you need one number per state (e.g., compare state-level maxima across regions) | Use as a pre-aggregated input when joining state-level metrics to other one-row-per-state datasets
params.output_schema: state_name: state name (s.state_name). This is the grouping key from the base table state.state_name. | max_city_population: maximum population among cities in that state (MAX(c.population)). Derived from cities_by_state_cohort.population aggregated with SQL MAX()
params.metric: max_city_population = MAX(cities_by_state_cohort.population)  -- computed per state_name
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-state dimension or view (for example a canonical state-level view keyed by state_name) on state_name — safe because this view has exactly one row per state_name, so its measure max_city_population will not be duplicated. | Safe to join to sibling view city_base only if that sibling is pre-aggregated to one row per state_name (otherwise do not join directly). | Do NOT join this AGG to any one-to-many table or view keyed by state_name (for example a table listing multiple state-level events, multiple counties per state, or a cities table with multiple rows per state) without first re-aggregating the downstream table to one row per state_name. Directly joining to one-to-many detail would multiply rows and therefore multiply or distort max_city_population. | If you need to combine this view with additional city-level measures (one row per city), instead: either (a) re-derive city-level measures and compute a new per-state aggregate alongside or instead of this view, or (b) aggregate the city-level data to one row per state (e.g., MAX, SUM, COUNT as appropriate) and then join to this view on state_name. | When composing into larger aggregated queries (e.g., region-level metrics), treat max_city_population as a state-level scalar that can be safely aggregated using aggregate functions appropriate for the new grain (for example, use MAX(max_city_population) to get the maximum city population across states in a region, or AVG(max_city_population) to get the average of state maxima). Avoid using SUM(max_city_population) unless summing per-state maxima is a meaningful metric for your use case.

views.name: city_rows_with_population
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.city_name AS city_name,
  city.population AS population,
  city.state_name AS state_name,

FROM city

params.description: Provides one row per city (where population is known) with that city's population and its state and country names.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve city-level population and location (state, country) for reporting or downstream joins. | Filter or slice city populations by state_name or country_name. | Compose city-level populations into higher-level aggregates (state, country) by aggregating this view. | Join to other dimension tables keyed by city_name to enrich city attributes (provided those joins are one-to-one).
params.output_schema: city_name: The city name (derived directly from city.city_name). | population: The city's population (derived directly from city.population). | state_name: The state name the city belongs to (derived directly from city.state_name). | country_name: The country name the city belongs to (derived directly from city.country_name).
params.metric: population = city.population (base column, not an aggregate in this view).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a state-level one-row-per-state dimension (e.g., state_city_population_agg if it is one-row-per-state) on state_name — safe because city_rows_with_population is one-row-per-city and joining to a one-row-per-state dimension will not duplicate city rows or the population measure. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a country-level one-row-per-country dimension on country_name — safe because the country dimension has one row per country, so city rows remain one-to-one with their country and population values are not duplicated. | do NOT join to any table or view that is one-to-many from city (for example a hypothetical table events_per_city with multiple event rows per city) without first aggregating that other table to one row per city (e.g., GROUP BY city_name) — otherwise the city population values would be multiplied by the number of matching rows in the other table. | do NOT join to sibling or other views that expand cities into multiple rows (for example a cohort or history view that lists repeated city rows across periods) unless you re-aggregate population appropriately. If you need to combine with such views, either (a) aggregate those views to one row per city before joining, or (b) aggregate population after the join using SUM(population) GROUP BY the desired grain, being mindful that population in this view is a point-in-time base column (not a pre-aggregated metric). | When composing upward aggregates (state or country totals), compute SUM(population) GROUP BY state_name or country_name from this view to avoid double-counting; do not rely on joining this view to a many-row state-level dataset without aggregation. | When joining on city_name, ensure the other side is one-row-per-city (or pre-aggregated to that grain). The view's grain is one-row-per-city (city_name), so safe joins preserve that cardinality.

views.description: Provides one row per city (where population is known) with that city's population and its state and country names.

views.name: cities_grouped_by_state_avg_population
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.state_name AS state_name,
  COUNT(c.city_name) AS city_count,
  AVG(c.population) AS avg_city_population
FROM city_rows_with_population c
WHERE c.population IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.state_name

params.description: Provides, per U.S. state name, the number of cities counted and the average population of those cities (excluding null populations).
params.when_to_use: Report the count of cities and average city population per state. | Compare states by average city population. | Compose higher-level aggregations by state (e.g., rank or percentile of avg_city_population) without re-scanning city rows. | Join state-level attributes (one-row-per-state) to enrich these state-level metrics.
params.output_schema: state_name: name of the state; derived from city_rows_with_population.state_name | city_count: integer count of city_name values in the state (excludes rows where population IS NULL because of the view's WHERE clause but counts still uses city_name); derived from COUNT(city_rows_with_population.city_name) | avg_city_population: average of population over cities in the state excluding rows with population IS NULL; derived from AVG(city_rows_with_population.population)
params.metric: city_count = COUNT(city_rows_with_population.city_name)  -- cardinality metric: number of city_name occurrences per state (NULL city_name values would be excluded by COUNT semantics) | avg_city_population = AVG(city_rows_with_population.population)  -- mean population computed over rows where population IS NOT NULL (the view filters out NULL populations)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-state dimension (e.g., a states table or a view that is one-row-per-state keyed by state_name) on state_name — safe because this view is one-row-per-state so its measures (city_count, avg_city_population) will not be duplicated. | Do NOT join this view directly to city-level or other one-to-many tables/views keyed by state_name (for example, joining back to city_rows_with_population, city_base, or any city-level view) without first re-aggregating those tables to the state_name grain. Such joins would multiply rows for a state and thus incorrectly scale city_count and avg_city_population. | If you need to combine city-level detail with these state aggregates, either: (a) re-aggregate the city-level source to state_name and then join on state_name (ensures measures remain correct), or (b) join on state_name and immediately re-compute aggregates from the combined detail (i.e., ignore this view's aggregates and compute fresh aggregates after the join). | Safe composition with sibling views: joining to other one-row-per-state sibling aggregates (for example, state_city_population_agg if it is also one-row-per-state) on state_name is safe. Avoid joining to sibling views that are at a finer grain (e.g., city_rows_with_population, city_base, or cities_by_state_cohort if it is cohorted per city) without aggregation.

views.name: state_basic_attributes
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state.state_name AS state_name,
  state.population AS population,
  state.area AS area,
  state.country_name AS country_name,
  state.capital AS capital,
  state.density AS density
FROM state

params.description: Provides one-row-per-state basic attributes (name, population, area, country, capital, and precomputed density).
params.when_to_use: Retrieve state-level attributes for display, filtering, or joining to other state-grain data. | Compose higher-level SQL that aggregates, filters, or ranks states by population, area, or density. | Join state attributes to city-level data when you need state context (e.g., add state_name or country_name to city results) while avoiding duplication by following cardinality guidance.
params.output_schema: state_name: The state's canonical name; comes from state.state_name | population: The state's total population (base column); comes from state.population | area: The state's land area (base column); comes from state.area | country_name: The country that contains the state; comes from state.country_name | capital: The name of the state's capital city; comes from state.capital | density: Population density for the state (precomputed); comes from state.density
params.grounded_columns: state.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name | state.capital | state.density
params.metric: population = state.population  -- base column, stored at state grain | area = state.area  -- base column, stored at state grain | density = state.density  -- precomputed metric stored on state; expected to equal population / area if derived
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimensional/state-grain views or tables on state_name — e.g., join to this view FROM another state-grain view ON state_name — safe because state_basic_attributes is one-row-per-state so its measures are not duplicated. | Safe: join to sibling view state_city_population_agg (AGG) on state_name — safe because that AGG should be aggregated to state grain; confirm the sibling AGG is one row per state before joining to avoid duplication. | Safe: join to cities_grouped_by_state_avg_population (AGG) on state_name — safe only if that sibling view is aggregated to one row per state; otherwise aggregate first. | Do NOT directly join state_basic_attributes to one-to-many detail tables or selects that output multiple city rows per state (for example: city_base, city_rows_with_population, or cities_by_state_cohort) without re-aggregating the detail side back to state grain first, because those joins will multiply state_basic_attributes' population/area/density measures and produce incorrect totals or averages. | If you must combine with city-level tables, either: (a) aggregate the city table up to state_name (e.g., SUM(city.population) GROUP BY state_name) and then join on state_name, or (b) join and then use window functions or DISTINCT ON patterns that maintain one row per state, depending on the desired calculation. | When composing metrics: prefer deriving new state-level metrics by aggregating city-level data separately and then joining to state_basic_attributes on state_name, rather than summing state_basic_attributes after a one-to-many join. | Key uniqueness guarantee: this view's grain is state_name (one row per state_name) because each output column is selected directly from the state table without aggregation; treat state_name as the primary key for safe joins and composition.

params.description: Provides one row per city with that city's name, population, and the state's name — useful for listing city-level attributes and building city-level analysis.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve city-level attributes (name, population, state) for display, reporting, or filtering. | Compose city-level filters or joins when building higher-level aggregates (e.g., rollups by state) by using this view as the city input. | Seed queries that need a stable, one-row-per-city grain to join to other 1:1 or many:1 dimensions without duplicating city measures.
params.output_schema: city_name: City name string — derived directly from base table column city.city_name | population: City population (raw value) — derived directly from base table column city.population | state_name: State name string for the city — derived directly from base table column city.state_name
params.metric: population = <base column: city.population>  -- not an aggregate in this view; it is a raw measure at the city grain
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE joins: join to a state-level one-row-per-state view (for example state_basic_attributes or state_city_population_agg when aggregated to state) on key city.state_name = state_basic_attributes.state_name — safe because city_core is one-row-per-city and state views are one-row-per-state, so joining will not duplicate state-level rows (it will expand state rows to many cities as intended). | Cardinality-SAFE joins: join to other one-row-per-city normalized views (e.g., city_base or city_rows_with_population if they are also one-row-per-city) on city_core.city_name = city_base.city_name — safe because both sides are at the same grain (1:1), so measures from city_core will not be multiplied. | Do NOT join cardinality-unsafe to one-to-many detail tables or views (for example, a hypothetical table of city_events or any view that has multiple rows per city, or an AGG sibling that is aggregated by a different grain without re-aggregation) without re-aggregating the detail side first. Joining city_core (one-row-per-city) directly to a one-to-many table on city_name will multiply city_core population values across the many matching detail rows and thus distort sums/averages unless you either: |   - pre-aggregate the one-to-many table to one row per city before joining, or |   - aggregate after the join back to the desired grain, ensuring correct aggregation functions are used (e.g., SUM(detail_metric) GROUP BY city_core.city_name and then join), | Avoid joining to AGG views that are aggregated at a different grain (for example, cities_grouped_by_state_avg_population which is aggregated to state) unless you join on the appropriate state key and understand that the AGG view's measures are already aggregated; do not join state-aggregated measures to city rows expecting them to remain at state granularity without duplicating or re-aggregating appropriately. | Practical guidance for planners: treat city_core as canonical one-row-per-city source. Allowed safe patterns: 1) city_core ⟷ city-level dimension (1:1), 2) city_core ⟶ state-level aggregation (many cities per state) when rolling up (aggregate city measures by state after joining). Unsafe without re-aggregation: city_core ⟷ detail tables with multiple rows per city (1:many) — would multiply city_core.population if joined directly and then summed.

views.name: state_borders

SELECT state_name, border
FROM border_info

params.description: Lists state-to-border relationships: one row per state border (state name and the border identifier/name).
params.when_to_use: Find all borders for a given state (e.g., which states border Texas). | Compose higher-level aggregations about borders per state (e.g., count of borders per state) by aggregating this view. | Join state attributes to border records when analyzing border-level details (e.g., border-level policies or statistics stored in another table keyed by state+border). | Filter or subset states by border membership before joining to other state- or border-level data.
params.output_schema: state_name: the name of the state (derived directly from base column border_info.state_name) | border: an identifier or name of the border associated with the state (derived directly from base column border_info.border)
params.metric: No derived metrics/aggregates are defined in this view; both output columns are direct projections: state_name = border_info.state_name, border = border_info.border
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_basic_attributes (or any one-row-per-state view/table) on state_name — safe because state_basic_attributes is one-row-per-state, so joining state_borders (one row per state+border) to it will not duplicate measures from state_basic_attributes beyond the expected expansion to border-level rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_summary_basic (if it is one-row-per-state) on state_name — safe for the same reason as above; this view is at border granularity so state-level measures will be repeated per border intentionally but will not cause unintended multiplicative duplication of border rows. | NOT safe to join directly to city_base, city_core, city_rows_with_population, or any city-level view (one-to-many from state to city) on state_name without re-aggregation: doing so would multiply border rows by the number of cities in the state, causing measures counted at border granularity to be duplicated. To combine with city-level data, first aggregate the city-side to state or state+border level (e.g., city counts per state) and then join, or aggregate the joined result back to the desired grain. | NOT safe to join directly to states' aggregated views that are at a different granular aggregation (e.g., state_city_population_agg, cities_grouped_by_state_avg_population) unless you join on state_name and understand that those aggregated state-level metrics will be repeated per border row — if you need state-level metrics preserved without repetition, either join and then re-aggregate to state level or pre-embed the metrics into a one-row-per-state structure and join as described above. | When composing additional aggregations on top of this view (for example, COUNT(border) per state), treat this view as the detailed (detail = state+border) table: group by state_name to produce state-level metrics. Avoid joining other detail tables (e.g., cities) directly before aggregating, unless you intend to produce a combined detail-level rowset and handle de-duplication/aggregation explicitly.

views.name: city_population_classification
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_name AS city_name,
  c.population AS population,
  CASE
    WHEN c.population >= 50000 THEN 'High Population'
    WHEN c.population IS NOT NULL THEN 'Low Population'
    ELSE NULL
  END AS population_classification

FROM state s
